samples.question: The cream page carries small decorative coloured squares; they lie outside the dark slate board, none of them touches it, and none of them means anything. Everything that decides the answer is painted on that one slate BOARD. On the left of the board is the FIELD: a 7-by-7 arrangement of 49 square colour swatches, each swatch flat sand, teal, rose, olive or indigo. On the right of the same board, separated from the field by a wide slate gutter, is the KEY: a detached 3-by-3 patch of nine swatches drawn in the same five colours but at a visibly smaller cell size. A WINDOW is any 3-by-3 block of neighbouring field swatches; there are 25 windows and they overlap. Exactly one window has the same nine colours as the key, in the same arrangement, reading row by row; every other window differs from the key in at least one swatch. Size is not a clue: the key is smaller than the field swatches, so only the pattern of colours can be compared. Some field swatches carry a MARK: a small round dot of red, amber, cyan or violet lying on top of the swatch. A mark never changes the colour of the swatch it lies on, marks appear on swatches inside and outside the matching window, and the key patch never carries a mark, so the key alone cannot tell you any mark. The centre swatch of the matching window always carries exactly one mark. Where the board sits, where the matching window sits, how many marks there are and how often each mark colour appears carry no other information. What is the colour of the mark on the centre swatch of the one window that matches the key? Answer red, amber, cyan or violet.
